sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text: Zwijndrecht, across the river from Dordrecht, charges for parking in only a few places and has resisted extending it. The council adopted the parking tax ordinance for 2026 on 2 December 2025: paid street parking costs 2.20 euros an hour and the surcharge for unpaid parking is 82 euros; a resident permit costs 39 euros a year and visitor parking 1.10 euros an hour [0]. Paid parking runs Monday to Wednesday from 09:00 to 18:00 and Thursday to Saturday until 21:00, and is free on Sunday, at the Werf, Ringdijk, Maasplein, Veerplein, Zomerlust, Schuitenwal, Nieuwstraat, Marsdiep and part of Rotterdamseweg, with a two-hour maximum at Veerplein [1]. A permit ordinance of December 2024 allows up to two resident permits per dwelling and a waiting list once a zone maximum is reached [3]. Around the station there are four blue zones with a two-hour limit on weekdays from 08:00 to 16:00, with an unlimited exemption for residents at 46.60 euros a year [4]. The traffic plan says parking is facilitated but no more spaces are built than needed, aims at 90 to 100 percent occupancy, and records that paid parking at Walburg had been abolished [7]. Counts in 2018 found no area in the centre above 90 percent occupancy at any count moment, though some road sections exceeded 100 percent, and they may be out of date [8]. A savings paper of September 2024 proposed reintroducing paid parking at Walburg and around the station from 1 July 2025 for about 400,000 euros extra income, and the first management report of 2026 books nothing for that lever in 2026 to 2029 [5][6].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text: The development is about homes near the station. The parking rules for the Stationskwartier set norms of 0.5 to 1.1 spaces per dwelling, lowest for social rental flats near the station, and let each shared car reduce the requirement by six spaces [10]. A land-development document for Maasterras Oost of September 2025 assumes about 340 apartments and 277 parking spaces, 0.8 per dwelling, of which 44 in a built structure [14]. A council letter of March 2026 on the Koninginneweg and Afslag redevelopment, 147 new homes, lists 90 new public and 8 private parking spaces and says there will be 89 more spaces than now, which its own figures do not quite add up to, and no permit has been issued for any sub-plan [15]. In the Veerplein restaurant street the parking spaces will disappear to make room for terraces, and the waterfront promenade is to be laid out from January 2027 [13]. A draft retail study for Walburg notes that on a Monday afternoon the car park in front of the Albert Heijn was almost full while the large south-east car park was mostly empty, and lists free, good parking as a strength [16]. On charging, the municipality fixed the 2026 to 2030 map of potential sites after 289 resident comments, about 70 percent of the critical ones citing parking pressure [18]. The concession for south-west Netherlands was awarded on 26 August 2026 to TotalEnergies and Velian, with a tariff of about 0.30 euro per kWh against about 0.45 before for new points [17]. The 2027 budget gives 351 public charge points at the end of 2025 [19].

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
Q-Park lists the P+R Westelijke Parallelweg with 119 spaces, open round the clock, and no tariffs online [11]. The 2024 paper says the P+R is owned by ProRail [5]. The 2024 proposal, to raise the tariff by 10 percent and let the 32 annual passes lapse, 19 of them held by businesses, preceded the ordinance of December 2024 [2].

Our data cover the P+R Westelijke Parallelweg, with 119 spaces, for about 61 days since 22 August 2026. Occupancy averaged about 36% on weekdays and 13% at weekends, which fits a commuter car park, and it reached full in a single reading on a Monday morning. The paid streets and the shopping centres are not in our data.
